alerts.title: Strait of Hormuz disrupted since 28 February 2026

facts.text: The crisis began on 28 February 2026, when Iran's Revolutionary Guard warned ships off the strait after US and Israeli strikes; Iran announced the closure on 4 March. Reopening arrangements in April and June did not hold.

Trackers report the strait effectively closed to commercial shipping in November (3 transits on 8 November against about 85 a day before the crisis), while other estimates show oil flows partly restored. Traffic levels are contested.

About 70% of the Gulf's food imports normally pass through the strait. Importers have rerouted cargo through Fujairah, Khor Fakkan and Oman's Sohar, with onward trucking costing several times the ocean freight; Saudi Arabia has added Red Sea logistics corridors.
In March the UAE said its strategic reserve covers essential needs for up to six months. Retailers report using Fujairah, Saudi and neighbouring suppliers, chartered vessels and air freight.

Food inflation in Dubai reached 8.05% in September 2026, up from 7.39% in August. Prices of nine essential goods (cooking oil, eggs, dairy, rice, sugar, poultry, legumes, bread and wheat) cannot rise without ministry and national committee approval.

alerts.response: Monitor reserve cover and bypass-port throughput weekly for the nine price-approved staples, and give bypass capacity priority to the staples with the fewest supplier origins.
alerts.watch: Days of cover for the nine essential goods; throughput at Fujairah and Khor Fakkan; Dubai food inflation
exposureText: Only 2% of basket import tonnes came from neighbours reachable by road (Saudi Arabia and Oman) in 2023; the rest normally arrived by sea, most of it through the strait.

alerts.title: Sugar: world price surge and Indian export ban

facts.text: India moved raw, white and refined sugar exports to 'prohibited' in May 2026 until 30 September 2026, with limited quota carve-outs.

For the 2026-27 season only a 5,841-tonne EU quota has been confirmed (DGFT, October 2026); whether the general ban continues is unconfirmed. India imposed domestic stock limits from 15 October to 30 November 2026 as ex-mill prices rose.

alerts.response: Secure forward supply from the main origin and qualify a second origin; watch retailer margins under the price-approval rule, since sugar is one of the nine controlled staples.
alerts.watch: Effective suppliers of sugar; world sugar price; Indian export policy for 2026-27
exposureText: India supplied 13% of the UAE's imports of sugar in 2023; the leading origin was Brazil (78%).
The world sugar benchmark stood at 0.43 $/kg in October 2026: up 39% since February 2026 and up 27% on a year earlier.

alerts.title: Chicken: Newcastle disease in Brazil's Santa Catarina

facts.text: Brazil confirmed Newcastle disease on a commercial farm in Santa Catarina on 18 October 2026. Mexico suspended all Brazilian poultry, then narrowed the ban to Santa Catarina; Saudi Arabia, China and Chile restricted Santa Catarina only.
No UAE restriction was reported in the sources checked.

alerts.response: Confirm which Brazilian states supply UAE chicken and prepare state-level (regionalised) acceptance, as Saudi Arabia applied, so that a nationwide suspension is not needed.

brief.title: UAE food security: decision brief
brief.subtitle: Draft for FAO analyst review · November 2026
brief.preparedBy: Policy Intelligence pilot (FAO Subregional Office for the GCC States and Yemen) - draft, not an official assessment

parts: Day 263 of the Strait of Hormuz disruption, which began on 28 Feb 2026. About 70% of Gulf food imports normally pass through the strait; cargo is being rerouted through Fujairah, Khor Fakkan and Sohar at higher cost. Only 2% of the UAE's staple imports came from neighbours reachable by road in 2023.

Food inflation in Dubai reached 8.05% in September 2026. World prices have risen since February 2026: sugar +38.7%, wheat +23.1% and rice +19.6%. The government reported strategic reserves of up to six months in March; replenishment through bypass routes is now the decisive unknown.

items: Strait of Hormuz disrupted since 28 February 2026 (critical). Only 2% of basket import tonnes came from neighbours reachable by road (Saudi Arabia and Oman) in 2023; the rest normally arrived by sea, most of it through the strait.
Sugar: world price surge and Indian export ban (high). India supplied 13% of the UAE's imports of sugar in 2023; the leading origin was Brazil (78%).
Chicken: Newcastle disease in Brazil's Santa Catarina (watch). Brazil supplied 80% of the UAE's imports of chicken meat in 2023, with 1.53 effective suppliers in all.

Set up a weekly supply-and-reserve monitor for the nine price-approved staples: days of cover, bypass-port throughput and prices from the Essential Goods Prices Platform. FAO can support the design and indicators.
Secure second origins and forward supply for the staples with the fewest suppliers (chicken meat, sugar and rice), routed through bypass ports.

Protect affordability for lower-income households as food inflation reaches 8%: the price-approval rule caps shelf prices but shifts rerouting costs onto suppliers, which is hard to sustain for months.

parts: Keep essential food prices stable, enhance local production, halve food loss and waste by 2030 and enhance food safety and quality show delivery in the last six months. Diversify food import sources and build alternative supply and the National Programme to Strengthen Supply Chain Resilience are moving: agreements, rules or financing, but no operations or results reported in six months.
The National Programme to Strengthen Supply Chain Resilience was approved in April 2026; latest related step:

items: Market and price monitoring methods and indicators for staples under supply stress.
Trade-policy analysis of supplier-country restrictions and their exposure for the UAE.
Food loss and waste measurement aligned with SDG 12.3, to give the 2030 target a baseline.
Food balance and data-system support so that strategy indicators can be tracked between crises.

annexNote: Draft prepared for FAO analyst review. It is not an official FAO or UAE Government assessment.
Sources: FAOSTAT trade matrix (to 2023), World Bank commodity prices (to October 2026), the monitored policy record, and press and official sources listed in the pilot's alert log.
Exposure figures are based on UAE-reported import tonnes, which include re-exports.

supply.statusLabel: At risk against the 3-5 source benchmark
analysis: In 2023, ten of the 17 basket categories drew on the equivalent of three or more equally sized suppliers, the lower end of the strategy's 3-5 source benchmark. Eggs fell just short.

Six categories depend on fewer than two effective suppliers: rapeseed (Australia, 81% of tonnes), chicken meat (Brazil, 80% of tonnes), sugar (Brazil, 78% of tonnes), barley (Australia, 75% of tonnes), rice (India, 73% of tonnes) and onions (India, 70% of tonnes). For these, one disruption at the dominant origin, whether an export ban, a harvest failure or a shipping closure, would remove most of the supply at once.

Concentration also reaches inputs: rapeseed, which supplies local edible-oil crushing. Expanding local production does not remove import risk; part of it moves upstream to the inputs that production needs.
Since 2018, diversification widened for potatoes, vegetable oils, soybean meal and beef and narrowed for fruit, eggs, barley and rapeseed.
supply.method: Effective number of suppliers = 1 / (sum of squared supplier shares of import tonnes), the inverse Herfindahl-Hirschman index: it equals the number of equally sized suppliers that would give the same concentration. Based on UAE-reported imports, which include goods later re-exported. The strategy's own method for counting "sources" is not published, so this is an analytical proxy.
supply.evidence: Implementation continues at a quickening pace (33 measures in the last 12 months against 26 in the 12 before; latest 9 Nov 2026).

options.action: Prioritise alternative-origin agreements for rapeseed, chicken meat and sugar
options.why: Effective suppliers below 2; top origin holds 81% of rapeseed, 80% of chicken meat and 78% of sugar.
options.watch: Effective number of suppliers rising to 3 or more

options.action: Bring production inputs into the food basket and the reserve plan
options.why: Rapeseed (local edible-oil crushing) is supplied by very few origins.

options.action: Publish the official basket and the method for counting sources
options.why: The 18-item basket and the measurement method are not public, so progress against goal 3 cannot be verified externally.
options.watch: Official basket list and source-count method released

analysis: Local production covers a growing share of supply for tomatoes (from 10% in 2015 to 38% in 2023), milk (from 8% in 2015 to 13% in 2023), fish and seafood (from 24% in 2015 to 29% in 2023) and other vegetables (from 22% in 2015 to 26% in 2023).
Self-sufficiency fell for dates (136% to 105%) and sheep and goat meat (74% to 48%), as demand grew faster than output.

Wheat and potatoes remain almost entirely imported. Field staples are structurally constrained by water, so their security rests on the supply pillar, not on this one; the gains are in tomatoes, milk and fish and seafood.

A strategy update reported in October 2026 aims for domestic production to meet 50% of crop needs (press-reported; not used for the status). On FAO balances the tracked crops supplied 14% of their combined domestic supply locally in 2023, or 30% leaving cereals aside. The distance to the target therefore depends mostly on whether cereals are counted, which the published update must make explicit.
FAO's food balances for the UAE are largely imputed or estimated (616 values flagged I, 56 values flagged E), so levels are indicative; the direction of travel is more reliable than any single value.
production.method: Self-sufficiency ratio = production / domestic supply quantity (FAOSTAT food balances, thousand tonnes). Where FAOSTAT records no production row, production is taken as zero.
production.evidence: Implementation continues at a steady pace (89 measures in the last 12 months against 94 in the 12 before; latest 9 Nov 2026).

options.action: Set and publish measurable local-production targets per basket item
options.why: The published aims ("enhance local production") carry no numeric target, so progress cannot be judged against intent.

options.action: Track the water cost of new production capacity
options.why: Gains are in water-intensive protected horticulture and dairy; expansion and water strategy need a common metric.
options.watch: Water use per tonne for new projects

preparedness.statusLabel: High structural exposure (reserve levels not public)
analysis: Cereal import dependency stands at 100% (2021-2023): virtually every tonne of grain is imported.
The food import bill is about 4% of merchandise exports (2022-2024), so the constraint is not the ability to pay; it is physical access when trade routes or origins are disrupted.
Food price inflation was 1.0% in December 2025, the latest month FAOSTAT publishes for the UAE; it is the affordability signal to watch during a supply shock.

With ability to pay strong and import dependence near total, reserve depth (days of cover per staple) becomes the decisive preparedness indicator. It is not published, so this pillar can be assessed only on exposure, not on readiness.
preparedness.method: FAOSTAT suite of food security indicators (3-year averages) and FAOSTAT consumer price indices.
preparedness.evidence: Implementation continues at a quickening pace (26 measures in the last 12 months against 12 in the 12 before; latest 25 Oct 2026).

options.action: Agree a confidential reserve-cover indicator with the government
options.why: Exposure is near total for cereals; without reserve data, readiness cannot be assessed.
options.watch: Days of cover per staple (restricted reporting)

options.action: Run a disruption stress test on the concentrated categories
options.why: Concentrated categories lose most of their supply if one origin fails.
options.watch: Months of supply covered by alternative origins

preparedness.owner: Ministry of Climate Change and Environment (MOCCAE)

analysis: The national target is to halve food loss and waste by 2030 (press-reported; official document pending). No baseline has been published, so neither the starting level nor progress can be measured.

The national baseline study was due to report in the first half of 2026; no published results were found. FAO's modelled estimate of retail losses for the UAE is a fixed parameter rather than a measurement and is not used here.
waste.method: Target from the register; no outcome series is available.
waste.evidence: Implementation continues at a quickening pace (9 measures in the last 12 months against 5 in the 12 before; latest 21 Oct 2026).

options.action: Obtain the baseline study results and adopt them as the tracking baseline
options.why: Without a baseline, a 50% reduction target cannot be monitored.

safety.statusLabel: No comparable outcome indicator - implementation only
analysis: International datasets carry no comparable food-safety outcome measure for the UAE, so this pillar is tracked through implementation only.

Nutrition outcomes bear on the "quality" side of the aim. Adult obesity is 31.6% (2024), about twice the world average of 16.2%; anaemia among women of reproductive age is 28.2% (2023), below the world average of 30.7%. The obesity burden is the clearest quality gap, and supply-side goals do not address it.
safety.method: FAOSTAT suite of food security indicators.
safety.evidence: Implementation continues at a steady pace (36 measures in the last 12 months against 42 in the 12 before; latest 26 Oct 2026).

options.action: Add nutrition outcomes to the strategy indicator set
options.why: Adult obesity at 31.6% is about twice the world average of 16.2%; the published goals carry no nutrition outcome.
options.watch: Obesity and anaemia trends against a stated target
